article_title: GitHub Restructures Bug Bounty Program, Cutting Public Payouts in Half and Reserving Top Rewards for a New VIP Tier
summary: Duplicate coverage: PR #2017 (identical GitHub bug-bounty-restructuring story) was merged and published to main before this review concluded. Rejected under duplicate-coverage policy regardless of this submission's own quality.

findings.details: PR #2017 ('GitHub Cuts Public Bug Bounty Payouts by Half, Moves Top Rewards Behind a New Invite-Only VIP Tier') covers the identical underlying story from largely the same primary sources (GitHub Blog x2, The Hacker News, curl/Daniel Stenberg blog posts). PR #2017 was merged at 2026-07-23T10:02:25Z (commit 60e73d895) and published at commit a029e801e ('Publish: GitHub Cuts Public Bug Bounty Payouts by Half, Moves Top Rewards Behind a New Invite-Only VIP Tier'), both on main, before this review reached a final verdict. Publishing this submission as well would duplicate coverage of a story already live on the site.

findings.message: VIP-tier payout claim overgeneralizes; false for Low and Medium severities
findings.details: Body states VIP payouts ($1,000/$7,500/$20,000/$30,000+ for low/medium/high/critical) are 'matching or exceeding the top of the old public ranges.' Per source-1 (The Hacker News), the old public ceilings were Low $2,000, Medium $10,000, High $20,000, Critical $30,000+. The VIP figures only match or exceed the old ceiling for High and Critical; the VIP Low ($1,000) and Medium ($7,500) payouts are actually LOWER than the old public ceilings ($2,000 and $10,000 respectively). This is a subordinate claim, not headline/lead, and would independently have warranted APPROVE_WITH_CORRECTIONS with a corrections filing had this submission not been rejected as a duplicate. Noted here for completeness since a comparable error was independently flagged by the PR #2017 reviewer.

content_preview.title: GitHub Restructures Bug Bounty Program, Cutting Public Payouts in Half and Reserving Top Rewards for a New VIP Tier
content_preview.summary: Effective July 27, GitHub is cutting public bug bounty payouts and creating an invite-only VIP tier, following curl's earlier bounty collapse under AI-generated reports.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

GitHub is overhauling its bug bounty program, cutting public payouts by at least half at every severity level while creating a permanent, invite-only tier that pays significantly more, according to a [GitHub Blog post](https://github.blog/security/next-chapter-restructuring-githubs-bug-bounty-program/) published July 22. The changes take effect July 27, and the company says they are meant to address what it calls "an increasing queue" of submissions, [GitHub wrote](https://github.bl...

recommendations: Do not rewrite or resubmit this submission — the topic is now covered by the published article from PR #2017. Per v3.9.0 policy, REJECT discards the work; the bot should not attempt another submission on this story.

Consider adding daniel.haxx.se to config/source_allowlist.txt — it is Daniel Stenberg's (curl lead maintainer's) primary-source engineering blog and is likely to recur as a legitimate citation in future open-source/security coverage.

Independent of the duplicate-coverage rejection: if this had been the surviving submission, the VIP-tier 'matching or exceeding the top of the old public ranges' claim would have needed a corrections filing, since it is false for Low and Medium severities.

editor_notes.content_quality: On pure editorial merit this was a strong, well-organized 1141-word Analysis piece (within the 800-2000 word range) with clear section structure (Overview, What's Changing, The May Preview, The curl Precedent, Analysis, What We Don't Know). Neutral, professional tone throughout; no sensationalism, no AI self-reference. Every direct quote is verbatim from its cited source and every specific dollar figure, date, and percentage traces to a cited source. This assessment is preserved here for the record even though the final verdict is REJECT for an unrelated reason (duplicate coverage, see below).
editor_notes.source_verification: chief:review fetched and saved all 5 sources; manifest.json reported all 5 at HTTP 200 with no errors and no archive_fallback flags. I decompressed and sha256-verified all 5 snapshots against the manifest — all 5 hashes matched exactly (source-0: b3d8e13d..., source-1: 78a49aed..., source-2: 1d4b20a0..., source-3: 59d442b0..., source-4: 4596cb55...), confirming no post-save corruption. However, manual inspection of the decompressed HTML revealed that 3 of the 5 snapshots captured the WRONG page despite the 200/hash-match: source-0.html.gz (nominally https://github.blog/security/next-chapter-restructuring-githubs-bug-bounty-program/) contained an unrelated ad/content-recommendation mashup (Xbox Wire, linuxiac.com Jellyfin, CBS News France social-media-ban content — zero occurrences of 'github' or 'bug bounty' in the text); source-2.html.gz (nominally https://daniel.haxx.se/blog/2026/01/26/the-end-of-the-curl-bug-bounty/) contained an unrelated GitHub issue page ('Rename the app #609 · andrewrabert/jellium-desktop'); source-3.html.gz (nominally https://daniel.haxx.se/blog/2026/04/22/high-quality-chaos/) contained an unrelated CSO Online article ('GitHub scales back bug bounties...', May 19, 2026, by Anirban Ghoshal). Only source-1.html.gz (The Hacker News, 'GitHub Cuts Public Bug Bounty Payouts, Moves Top Rewards to VIP Tier' by Swati Khandelwal) and source-4.html.gz (GitHub Blog, 'Raising the bar: Quality, shared responsibility...' by Jarom Brown, May 15 2026) matched their claimed URLs and content. This is a snapshot-fetcher infrastructure failure (wrong content served/cached despite a 200 status), not a fault of the contributor bot. Per skill Step 3b, I fell back to live WebFetch for the three mismatched URLs to independently verify the article's claims: WebFetch of https://github.blog/security/next-chapter-restructuring-githubs-bug-bounty-program/ confirmed verbatim: the new public payout table ($250/$2,000/$5,000/$10,000), the VIP table ($1,000/$7,500/$20,000/$30,000+), the qualification criteria (1 critical / 2 high / 4 medium / 7 low), the quotes 'Ranges sound flexible, but in practice they create uncertainty for researchers and overhead for our team,' 'You don't earn more by submitting more. You earn more by submitting better,' and 'an increasing queue,' the July 27 effective date, and the grandfathering of pre-July-27 reports. WebFetch of https://daniel.haxx.se/blog/2026/01/26/the-end-of-the-curl-bug-bounty/ confirmed verbatim: the January 31, 2026 program end date, the confirmed-vulnerability rate falling from 'somewhere north of 15%' to 'below 5%,' and the phrase 'explosion in AI slop reports.' WebFetch of https://daniel.haxx.se/blog/2026/04/22/high-quality-chaos/ confirmed verbatim: curl's March 2026 return to HackerOne and the quote 'once we had figured out that GitHub was not good enough,' submission volume 'about double the rate we had through 2025,' the confirmed rate recovering to 'somewhere in the 15-16% range,' 'Almost every security report now uses AI to various degrees,' and 'The slop situation is not a problem anymore.' Every claim, quote, date, and figure in the article checked out against either the correctly-fetched snapshots (sources 1 and 4) or the live-fetched fallback (sources 0, 2, 3). I also confirmed the article's internal cross-link (/article/2026-02/22-ai-generated-slop-is-overwhelming-open-source-projects-forcing-emergency-countermeasures) resolves to a real, previously-published article at that exact path.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: No hallucinated quotes and no fabricated specifics found across either directly-read or WebFetch-verified sources. One overgeneralization identified (see Accuracy finding above): the claim that VIP payouts 'match or exceed the top of the old public ranges' holds for High/Critical but is false for Low/Medium, where VIP pay is actually below the old public ceiling. This is a subordinate claim, not the headline/summary/lead.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and professional throughout. Both GitHub's framing and outside skepticism (the 'harder to assess' paragraph in Analysis, the open questions in 'What We Don't Know') are represented. No loaded language or editorializing beyond what is clearly marked as the Analysis section's interpretive framing.
